items.title: Despite paying tariffs, Americans are losing big on trade under Trump. The July U.S. trade deficit soared over 24% to $88.4 billion. That's the largest monthly deficit since the tariff front-running month of March 2025. The deficit in July 2024 under Biden was just $78.8 billion.
items.content:

items.title: Fed Governor Waller said if there's "continued progress toward our 2 per cent goal," he'd support keeping interest rates on hold. But inflation has made no progress in returning to 2% in years. Warsh said inflation has been too high, and Waller seems OK with letting it stay high.

items.title: Fed Governor Waller said he's inclined to keep rates on hold, but if inflation comes in hot, he'd "consider" a rate hike. Considering a hike is not the same as committing to an actual rate hike. Plus, a quarter-point hike will do nothing to cool inflation. Gold is up over $100.

items.title: Many are dismissing the rise in Treasury yields as not reflecting a problem with the U.S., as rising yields are a global phenomenon. But this overlooks the fact that the U.S. is not the only country to have issued too much debt and which will resort to inflation to repudiate it.

items.title: If strong economic growth is the reason Treasury yields are rising, why is the yield on Swiss Government 10-year bonds still under 45 basis points, about the same level as four years ago? If it’s just about governments competing for capital, Swiss yields should be rising too.

items.title: It's ridiculous to claim that Treasury yields aren't rising due to increased inflation expectations, a loss of confidence in U.S. fiscal policy, declining Fed credibility and questions over its independence, or de-dollarization, as those are the most obvious reasons for the rise.

items.title: The average yield on 10-year Treasuries during the 1980s was 10.6%, and during the 1990s it was 6.7%. Yields should be higher now as we are a much worse credit risk given the size of our debt and the rate at which it's increasing. So the current 4.8% yield won't stay this low.

items.title: If a 4.8% yield on a 10-year Treasury seems high, during the 1970s the average yield was 7.5%. During that decade the national debt averaged about $500 billion, 1/80th of its present size. Yes, inflation as measured by the now rigged CPI was higher then, but that'll soon change.

items.title: Gold sold off on the belief the Fed will raise interest rates to fight inflation. In the unlikely event the Fed actually follows through, it'll lose the fight. Though nominal rates may rise, real rates will fall as inflation soars. That's bullish for gold.

items.title: Even if the Fed hikes rates, markets will immediate price in the next one. Since rate hikes will be big enough to weaken the economy, raise unemployment, and grow federal deficits, but too small to stop inflation from rising, the Fed may conclude rate hikes aren't worth the risk.

items.title: The 10-year Treasury yield is above 4.8%. The 30-year yield is near 5.3%. While these yields may seem high relative to what we've experienced in the recent years, given historic averages and the much larger size of our debt, they're actually still low and have a long way to rise.

items.title: The yield on Japanese 10-year government bonds hit 3% today, for the first time in 30 years. I forecast this on my podcast when the BOJ drew a line in the sand at 50 basis points. This is a huge problem for Japan, but a harbinger of an even bigger problem for the U.S. Got Gold?
